speechtext: It is because we have a Liberal government, Larry.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO RESOLVE LABOUR PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Well, Madam Speaker, I feel happy that someone has taken a shot at me, I appreciate that. Perhaps some of these remarks are coming home to people who run businesses. The obligation of management has for too long been forgotten. The unions get blamed for everything. According to headlines you see in the press every day, the unions are running the country. All hon. members get letters from people who are not knowledgeable enough to realize that more than labour is running the country; it has to be a combination of labour, management and government.
Every time some difficulty crops up in Canada, or for that matter in North America or even in Europe, the government gets involved. Why cannot labour problems be settled at the bargaining table where they are supposed to be settled? Honest bargaining, with the realization of the needs of management and the needs of labour, is what we need.
Much has been said today about the strike of the postal workers and the problems facing the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey), indeed facing all of us. I heard a gentleman on television tonight who is a postal letter carrier. He has been working for the Post Office department since 1968, and he has been off work one day since that time. He explained on television tonight how the letter carriers were the most important postal workers because they realize their obligations. Perhaps somebody in the postal department in middle management had passed the time of day with him and said, "Jack, you are doing a good job". Or perhaps the lady down the street had said: "Boy, my mail is always on time, even when it rains, because I depend on my pension cheque and on letters from my children overseas". This is the kind of worker running the postal service, and we meet them every day.
Only a small percentage of postal workers are creating problems for the Post Office department. Ninety-five per cent of the workers are there working for us every day, but the remaining 5 per cent try to stir things up and make them all look bad, especially the hard workers.
Some labour unions are not really unions. Some years ago my brother, who is a school teacher, used to comment on the way the unions ran the country. Now after 15 years he is a member of a union. It is not called a union but an association. People today are now complaining about school teachers. Why did the school teachers have to get together? It was because the school boards could not sit down with them and talk to them on a man to man basis.

May 27, 1975
Labour Relations
As I say, this is partly the reason for labour trouble today, a failure by labour and management to communicate with each other on a man to man basis.
I realize another hon. member wishes to speak, Madam Speaker, so I shall conclude on this note. In this great country of ours we must realize that we have so much going for us. Our country is strong and proud, and this fact alone will make us even stronger. No country became great without facing many problems. We are one of the few countries of the world that got our flag from parliament; many others had to bleed for it. I say to the members of this House, thank God that we only have postal and other labour problems in this country today, and have not had to shed blood in order to stand under our flag.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO RESOLVE LABOUR PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am quite pleased to take part in this debate launched by my colleague for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne) who is a distinguished unionist well sensitized to the problems of workers who are now facing troubled times not only in Quebec but throughout Canada.
Needless to add, Madam Speaker, in the short time allowed to me that more than 3,351,390 man-days on average have been lost each year between 1960 and 1970 as a result of various strikes. Needless to add either that in several cases, the strike is not only legal but often justified, that is the workers have the right to strike and they are urged to do so. One only has to think, for example, of a strike which is now affecting my constituents in the furniture industry where, after 27 years of employment in the same dusty plant, even though they are practically artists, some cabinet makers or furniture finishers still earn $2.60 per hour, which is the new minimum wage in Quebec.
Generally speaking, one can say that in most cases, workers are peaceful people who want to better their lot, who do not want to break anything nor restrict the rights of others in our society. Unfortunately, these people are manipulated, lead by union leaders, who often abuse their power, their prestige, their title, compel workers by restricting their freedom and leading them to actions that everyone regrets in the end.
I do not refer necessarily to acts of violence, since these are exceptional. But when a strike has lasted two, three or four months in some sectors, how long will it take for the workers who were to be given help through the strike, because the strike weapon has been invented to defend the workers' rights in extreme circumstances, how long will it be before they return to normal conditions? Finally, the strike is not a peaceful means. It is an extreme means, once all other avenues have been unsuccessfully explored.
As my colleague from Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne) very rightly said, today, under the influence of union leaders, workers go on strike first and then, having demonstrated their strength, they go on to bargaining. While logic and common sense dictate that everything possible must be done to negotiate, if that does not succeed, legal mechanisms provide this extreme solution, the strike. Why do I say it is extreme? Because rarely does the worker, what-

ever increase he gained through this pressure action, recoup the amounts he lost during the strike.
That shows, Madam Speaker, that the main problem facing our society is not necessarily the strike mechanism, but rather the bargaining process that is defective. Indeed, everyone can strike in any circumstances. Today we have rotating, legal, wildcat, vertical, horizontal and all kinds of strikes. But what we fail to develop is our bargaining process which must precede any collective or common action called a strike. That is why my colleagues and I are for the right to strike. Because association is a human right, we cannot in any event deny that right derived from the right to associate and which is the counterpart of that of the employer. The motion we proposed today seeks especially to improve the bargaining process since it is at that exact level that the main problem lies.
For instance, to say that after two or four months negotiations have still not been held between employer and employee is ridiculous and the worker is always the victim. On a limited striking fund, he goes on strike and there are no negotiations. Finally, Madam Speaker, even this last resort means of protecting the worker's right works against him because he must bear the financial consequences. If we add abuse to that situation, on the one hand from union leaders who generally are associated with politicians-and here I have in mind the Parliament of Quebec which uses such gimmicks that there is no longer any form of union freedom-then the problem takes extreme proportions. Anyway, Madam Speaker, those union leaders who abuse their influence, call for violence, and rebellion against those in power are finally exploiting workers to create an unofficial government and challenge the very real strength of democracy invested in the duly elected representatives, so that we wake up in a state of permanent turmoil, of constant distrust, and God knows where we will end up. When faced with such situations of extreme abuses, Parliaments-and this one is no exception-are forced to step in often in turn in an extreme and abusive way, supposedly under the legitimate pretext of preserving the common interest. That is why this Parliament, including myself, has adopted special legislation to settle so-called exceptional situations. All of this, because the parties involved probably refused to bargain in respect, honesty, good will and good faith. This, however, as suggested by my colleague the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne), is probably due to the fact that our labour legislation, including our Canadian Labour Code, is outdated.
Madam Speaker, as this debate is coming to an end, I take the liberty of asking this question. Why are all Canadians and hon. members so anxious to streamline our democratic institutions, improve the financing of political parties, modernize and adapt all our legislation? There is no exception to this rule, whether it be in the fields of communications, culture, economy, finance, income tax- hon. members will readily remember the thorough tax reform that was adopted by the House.
Yet, for more than 25 years, only one area has not been updated, has not been improved, has not been adapted, and it is our Canadian Labour Code. It is the only area we are not really looking into in order to adapt our negotiation

and our arbitration methods to the modern conflicts which have modern causes, like automation.
I see the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) who is present and who is showing remarkable leadership in dealing with a conflict in postal services. Well, Madam Speaker, this proves once again that the minister's only way out is the recourse to the oldish grievance procedure which takes-and on this the union leaders are right- tremendous time. So, the postal workers have no other choice but to resort to violence and to voluntary exclude themselves from the democratic process, because they no longer believe in it, because it is outdated, because it takes too much time.
Madam Speaker, today we have moved this motion, which I find positive, and have asked our colleague from Kamouraska to do so because he knows this field. It is precisely to make Parliament fully aware of the situation of conflict we are constantly experiencing from sea to sea. I want to point out to my colleagues from the other provinces that those conflicts are not restricted to Quebec alone. It is imperative that we should notice it, and take this opportunity today to think positively and try to convince the minister that the act should be brought up to date in its widest sense that it might adapt to our modern times.
Madam Speaker, this is extremely important. Electronic automation is replacing man increasingly. More and more thought is being given to reducing work hours, to improving work conditions, to reducing the work week, precisely because the machine is replacing man.
In a second stage, after having modernized our negotiating institutions, we will inevitably have to tackle our social security system to guarantee an income to our workers who will have been replaced by the machine.
Madam Speaker, will we wait for the ridiculous situation where union leaders will ask to throw out the machines under the pretext of guaranteeing the worker job security?
How ridiculous for us to have reached that point! It proves that the source of the evil, for the workers, is the lack of income or income security, and not so much job security.
That is why, Madam Speaker, we are happy not only to have raised this debate but also to have heard useful comments from both sides of the House. This is the third time that we have launched such a debate in the House to speak of the sharing of employees in company benefits and to speak of unemployment, which is particularly acute among our young people who really wish to get satisfaction out of their work.
Contrary to many of our predecessors, Madam Speaker, this is our third attempt at raising the issue. We shall try and do so again later, but we are quite happy with today's reaction to the motion, hoping that it will contribute to the rallying of goodwill in Parliament as well as in the country, so that finally, all Canadians will unite to build their country and stop holding records for more man-days on strike than at work. Madam Speaker, when we have such a high unemployment rate in a country of our size with such a small population, we cannot allow ourselves, in a state of economic crisis such as the one we are now facing, to play
Adjournment Debate
the game of union leaders who abuse their powers or the game of some politicians who dream up gimmicks with union leaders.
That is why I feel the federal government should show leadership in this field.

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-REASON FOR FAILURE TO ADOPT STANDARDS FOR ASBESTOS FIBRES UNDER CLEAN AIR ACT-POSSIBLE PROTEST FROM UNITED STATES
ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-REASON FOR FAILURE TO ADOPT STANDARDS FOR ASBESTOS FIBRES UNDER CLEAN AIR ACT-POSSIBLE PROTEST FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on March 20 this year I asked a question of the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Sauve) which dealt with the problems relating to asbestos in this country. There are really two aspects to the question.
I asked first why the minister has not brought in regulations concerning asbestos under the Clean Air Act so we can have a national environmental standard in an effort to help to overcome the problem at Thetford Mines. I could also mention Cassiar Mines in British Columbia, Clinton

May 27, 1975
Adjournment Debate
Mines in the Yukon, and so on. The following is the answer in part given by the minister:
We are now looking into the asbestos question, and when we get together to regulate those standards the provinces, using their authority, will implement them.
With the greatest respect, it is my understanding that the minister under the Clean Air Act has jurisdiction to impose ambient air standards; that is, standards for the air outside enclosures. I suggest that she does not have to regulate in this regard through the provinces. She may have to consult with the provinces, but she does not have to wait for the provinces to take action. There is a consultation procedure, but the minister does have the jurisdiction to solve this very serious problem in the outer air.
This is a problem which we cannot treat lightly. I should like to read from some recent information. I shall quote from the Montreal Gazette of May 20, 1975. The headline is "Industry, doctors accused of cover-up in asbestos peril". It reads:
Brodeur, a New Yorker magazine writer and author of two books on lung diseases affecting asbestos workers, defined the 'medical-industrial complex' as an 'entrenched group of doctors working for industry and government'.
The article continues:
Brodeur said he has found it peculiar that, as far back as 1917, virtually all Canadian and American insurance companies were refusing to insure asbestos workers.
That was back in 1917. It has taken the medical profession, the government, and industry another 50 years to discover the danger of working in asbestos mines. I suggest this is really a national scandal that has gone on in respect of the asbestos mines.
Again I should like to quote from this article in the Montreal Gazette:
According to Brodeur, statistics have shown one in five workers exposed to asbestos dust particles dies of cancer or asbestosis.
There are also severe risks related to asbestos for those who work in the railroad industry. I should like to quote now from an article by Dr. Thomas F. Mancuso, an IAM medical consultant: He says:
The old time railroad machinists from every section of the country have independently described the asbestos dust exposure which centers on the steam locomotives; the use of asbestos to cover the steam boilers of the engines, ever since the steam engine and the railroad began. The pattern of work exposures and procedures were similar in all railroad shops in the country.
This is not something new. This is something which has been going on for many years, and yet governments have fallen fast asleep in regard to protecting workers from death by cancer simply because of the old productive wheel which had to keep turning regardless of the risk to those involved.
A second aspect of the question which was asked on March 20 dealt with information I had that the environmental protection agency operating from Maine had lodged a complaint with the Canadian government concerning ambient air which was blowing across the border from Thetford. I would be happy to be corrected because that information came to me through a radio broadcast. I see my hon. friend the parliamentary secretary smiling, so it could be that the information I had may not be correct. I have not been able to trace the source of that information.

I understood that there had been a problem and that an official protest had been made. It is probably fair to say that there was a problem, but whether an official protest was lodged may be in some doubt. I will let the parliamentary secretary deal with that.
I cannot, however, fail to feel somewhat outraged that the answer I received with regard to the imposition of clean air standards for asbestos is that we will see those standards before the end of this year. I submit that people will be injured and will suffer additional cancers before the end of this year, and in my view it is untenable that the government should not immediately impose ambient air standards right across the country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Len Marchand (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-REASON FOR FAILURE TO ADOPT STANDARDS FOR ASBESTOS FIBRES UNDER CLEAN AIR ACT-POSSIBLE PROTEST FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for bringing this important question before the House. He has been very consistent, and this is undoubtedly a very important matter which must be dealt with. I suppose there are many good reasons it has not been dealt with before now, but in all fairness the Clean Air Act is a pretty new piece of legislation which was passed by the parliament of Canada.
The air pollution control directorate of the Department of the Environment has been studying the problem of asbestos fibres in the air for some time. Meetings have been held with officials of the province of Quebec as well as with those industries involved in the mining and milling of asbestos. The Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Sauve) will be proposing to the governor in council national emission standard regulations for asbestos mining and milling operations prior to the end of this year. These regulations will allow control of stack emissions in both the mining and milling processes, as well as for fugitive dust emissions resulting from handling operations and waste disposal.
The regulations will be established under the Clean Air Act, and the provinces will be implementing the standard under their own authority. As a regulation under the Clean Air Act, however, the federal government can of course enforce the standard itself, should this prove necessary.
Officials of the Department of the Environment, of the Department of External Affairs and of the Canadian embassy in Washington are not aware of any protest being received from any U.S. authority concerning airborne asbestos fibres crossing into Maine. I was glad to hear that the hon. member was relating his information to a radio broadcast. I would like to know if he has any further information. We would be glad to follow it up.

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-SUGGESTED SEPARATE MINISTRY FOR CIVIL AIR TRANSPORT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
AIR TRANSPORT-SUGGESTED SEPARATE MINISTRY FOR CIVIL AIR TRANSPORT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, last month the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) indicated that a separate ministry for air transport was one of the aspects of transportation policy being considered. I want to point out this evening that over ten years ago the Glassco Commission considered this option, but the government of the day decided on a wider approach, a so-called co-ordinated policy embracing all
May 27, 1975

types of transport as they related to the economic growth of Canada. I suggest that it is time to re-assess the situation, particularly in view of the increasing complexities of the whole transportation question and the demands on the ministry as it now exists.
The duties of the Minister of Transport are spelled out, among other places, in the National Transportation Act, the Railway Act, the Pilotage Act, the Canadian National Railways Act, and the Aeronautics Act. They involve responsibility for certain aspects of rail, air, and sea travel, for northern transportation, and for the Canadian Transport Commission. Dredging contracts, airports, freight rates and so on, all are matters of concern to the Minister of Transport. Certainly this heavy workload has a direct relationship to the sorry state of affairs within the department. A separate department of air would relieve the burden somewhat, and seems particularly reasonable given the fact that the Department of Transport shows every sign of continuing to grow and, within it, the field of air transportation is one of the fastest growing elements.
Steadily growing expenditures are one indication of the growth of the ministry. The budget of the Department of Transport has increased by about 267 per cent in the last five years, from 354.2 million in 1970-71 to nearly one billion in 1975-76. Within this, the expenditures for air transportation have increased at a rate of 237 per cent, from 198.7 million to 471.3 million. Moreover, expansion of air passenger traffic is expected to continue at a rate of 8 per cent a year until 1978; while air cargo is presently growing at a rate of close to 18 per cent. This continued growth of air transportation presents a strong argument in favour of a separate ministry of air, particularly since the main argument against it-the need for a co-ordinated transportation policy-is inconclusive.
One of the things a minister of air or of civil aviation could do, for example, would be to reorganize the affairs of Air Canada. He could provide for a more flexible type of Crown corporation; he could direct an infusion of capital, and so on. In passing, Madam Speaker, I should like to point out that the debt-equity ratio which is now being used as a financial crutch by management is not entirely justified. The other side of the coin is the very favourable interest rates that have been of assistance to Air Canada in the past. I should like to observe also, Madam Speaker, that under a separate ministry sporadic and purely political interference in civil aviation could be replaced by steady supervision.
A new minister of air could co-ordinate civil aviation policies. The same minister would not be in charge of competing modes of transport and would focus responsibility for a national air policy through one department. A minister for aviation would thus have time to supervise activities and direct policies on this unique form of transport. He or she could thoroughly evaluate and give attention to regional air policies-rationalize them-lessen Air Canada's monopoly in some areas where smaller airlines could do better, and encourage Air Canada to do a better job on long haul domestic and international flights.
A recent article in the Ottawa Citizen of May 23 quotes an airline executive as saying;
Adjournment Debate
Sometimes 1 have to wonder where Air Canada ends off and the Ministry of Transport begins,
The article later quotes a regional airline president as follows;
The government should either let the airline completely alone or it should step in to enforce some sort of consistency,
I suggest, therefore, that the argument for a separate ministry of aviation is a sound one, and I urge the minister to give it considerable thought. Such a ministry could also pay greater attention to Air Canada's activities abroad which affect our trade patterns and our national interests. For example, Air Canada is getting a black eye because the strike of its employees in Paris has been allowed to drag on for over a month. There have been many unfortunate side effects, and a loss of revenue.
I hope the minister will accept my observation in the fashion in which they are offered-an open minded fashion. I recognize his problem, but I hope he recognizes and the government recognizes that problems must be solved sometimes by using innovative methods and procedures at least on a trial basis. Certainly there are arguments to be made against a separate ministry, but I hope the government will fully explore both sides and attempt to do something.
If the creation of the Solicitor General's portfolio from the area of responsibility held by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) could be justified in 1965, then surely there is just as much if not more need for a ministry of air vis-a-vis the general portfolio of transportation than there was, let's say for a separate portfolio for the RCMP and the penitentiaries approximately ten years ago. In the interest of keeping cabinet positions within manageable numbers, I suggest that the government should consider abolishing the Solicitor General's portfolio. The Department of Justice should be responsible for carrying out the work now performed by the Solicitor General (Mr. All-mand), and a new ministry of aviation should be established as an experiment.

As the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) indicated on earlier occasions, he hopes to be in a position in the not too distant future to indicate to the House the results of the current review of transportation policy. In the meantime I might mention that one of the requirements we see is the need to develop all modes of transport in an integrated way so that the best use is made of each mode in relation to others. The requirements of all modes can then be considered in a balanced way, by taking into consideration the requirements of users, carriers, and governments. The desirability of creating a separate ministry of aviation would have to be examined within this concept.
I should add, as a western Canadian, that I also look forward to the minister's announcement concerning the

new transportation policy. We, in western Canada, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) will no doubt agree, face many problems in transportation. We hope that a new transportation policy will soon be formulated and resolve many of our transportation problems.

subtopic: INCOME TAX-DECENTRALIZATION OF DATA PROCESSING- POSSIBLE ESTABLISHMENT OF OFFICE IN ATLANTIC REGION

speechtext:
Mb'. Andy Hogan (Cape Breton-East Richmond):
Madam Speaker, as recorded at page 5822 of Hansard for May 15, replying to my question concerning the criteria to be used in deciding on a location in the Atlantic region for the proposed data processing unit of his department, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Basford) noted several yardsticks he would use. These criteria included the number of tax returns filed with the Atlantic region, the availability of part-time and full-time workers, the availability of space, and the availability of communication links.
I want to develop some further observations on this matter this evening. I think the Sydney industrial area is an ideal location for such a data processing unit. We have an abundance of part-time workers available. Our latest unemployment figures for Cape Breton Island, as forwarded to me by the Nova Scotia department of labour, show unemployment rates for January, February, March and April of 13 per cent, 16.1 per cent, 17 per cent and 14.3 per cent respectively. These figures, of course, do not include the discouraged workers, male and female, who stopped looking for work because they considered it hopeless to do so. Besides that, our labour force participation rate for the first quarter of 1975 was 8 percentage points below that of Economic Region 6 in Nova Scotia, which includes Halifax County. Thus there is an abundance of underutilized human beings ready to work.
When it was announced that a satellite data processing centre was to be established in Winnipeg, it was noted that, initially at least, 125 highly skilled permanent jobs plus 1,000 part-time jobs would be created, with a 1975 payroll of $4 million.
I want the minister to know that the Nova Scotia Eastern Institute of Technology in my riding now teaches data processing. They are capable of training most of the highly skilled personnel needed, as well as the part-time people. We, through the Cape Breton Development Corporation and/or the College of Cape Breton, can provide adequate space; I think the minister would find the communications links more than suitable.
When the Department of Regional Economic Expansion was decentralized a couple of years ago, 84 members of the department were stationed in Moncton, 43 in Halifax, 41 in Fredericton, 19 in Charlottetown and 41 in St John's, Newfoundland.
As Nova Scotians we were happy to see the Halifax-Dartmouth metropolitan area profit from a special agreement entered into between the province of Nova Scotia and DREE. In Halifax a total of $87.7 million was earmarked for waterfront development, including a new, large hotel in downtown Halifax.

Some in Cape Breton thought it was an anomaly to build another luxury hotel in Halifax when our housing problem is so acute in Cape Breton, but the development of Halifax has helped Cape Breton in that many Cape Bretoners- they never call themselves ex-Cape Bretoners-can get steady jobs there.
We all hope that the metropolitan area growth investment scheme will be successful, and we are glad to note that following DREE's announcement of the special grant to the Halifax-Dartmouth area that One Sackville Place Ltd. of Halifax said it would build a $5 million low-profile eight storey building in Halifax on a 40,000 square foot site adjacent to the Hotel Nova Scotian owned by the Canadian National Railways.
It is time for some government agencies to be decentralized in favour of high unemployment areas, especially when they have almost 20 per cent of a provincial population as does Cape Breton county.
Surely it is unfair to let such areas try to fight the cold winds of international competition in their basic industries when all that is needed is the political will to make the government department decentralization process a tool of diversification and growth for such hard hit areas. I appeal to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) to take a strong stand with the Minister of National Revenue and other cabinet colleagues on this matter, which I consider a matter of principle as well as being an important means of getting balanced provincial development.
Mb'. Len Marchand (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment): Madam Speaker, the hon. member's question in the House on May 15, followed by the remarks which he has just concluded, arise from an announcement the minister made in Winnipeg on May 9.
On that occasion he announced the government's decision to carry out a geographic decentralization of the Ottawa Data Centre for the processing of income tax returns. The first of the satellite data centres is being established in Winnipeg. Within a period of up to five years, similar data centres-all linked to the central facility in Ottawa-will be established in the other four regions of Canada, that is in the Atlantic provinces, Quebec, Ontario, and the Pacific region.
I should mention that even before this important decision was made, the department, both on the taxation and the customs and excise sides, was one of the most decentralized of government departments. For instance, more than 80 per cent of the taxation employees are situated outside the capital.
I realize the big pitch the hon. member is making here tonight is important, namely, that these centres should be located in the slow growth areas of the country. I should also mention that very strong representations have been made to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Basford) by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen). All that the Minister of National Revenue can honestly say at this stage is that he is listening to all the representations being made to him. He has also mentioned
May 27, 1975

that representations were received from the other maritime provinces.
Our first regional data centre should be in operation by late 1975. In support of what I have said about the effect on the local labour force, I might mention that the Win -
Adjournment Debate
nipeg facility will require approximately 125 full-time and more than 1,000 casual employees during 1975-76. The 1976 payroll will exceed $3,800,000. It is a very important policy in many ways.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.26 p.m.
